These Are The Most Common Symptoms Doctors Are Seeing Right Now. It’s the start of sick season throughout the United States. By Jillian Wilson Senior Wellness Reporter, HuffPost Oct 1, 2026, 07:00 AM EDT |Updated Oct 1, 2026 11 Comments LOADINGERROR LOADING It’s that time of year. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, rates of norovirus, a nasty illness that causes gastrointestinal upset, are increasing throughout the United States. “It is the season when it increases,” said Catherine Troisi, an infectious disease epidemiologist at UTHealth Houston. “It’s around all the time, but cases typically increase ... late fall to winter, probably because people are indoors.” This allows the virus to spread more easily. Advertisement “Typically, we see it in two scenarios. The first is in outbreaks from a common exposure, such as when you hear about a lot of people on a cruise ship coming down with nausea and vomiting,” Dr. Donald Dumford, an infectious disease doctor at Cleveland Clinic, told HuffPost via email. “The second is sporadic cases, which seem to be more common in the winter months.” The virus tends to be common in nursing homes, too, and also often happens when people eat raw oysters. “It’s not necessarily surprising to start to see a rise at this time of year. Outside of those common source outbreaks, such as cruise ships, norovirus is also known as winter vomiting disease,” added Dumford. “We see a usual rise in cases throughout the winter months.” Advertisement The illness seems to spread more easily in cooler temperatures, he added, “and is able to survive longer on surfaces during that period of time.” Norovirus can cause very unpleasant symptoms. Norovirus tends to cause nausea and vomiting, and can also cause fever and diarrhea, Dumford said. Most people are sick for one to three days and recover fine at home, according to Troisi. (Be sure to stay hydrated if you do get sick.) It can last longer, though, and can lead to complications that require medical attention. “If you start to get fevers, blood in your stool, then call your healthcare provider as those can be signs of a more invasive type of gastrointestinal infection that may need antibiotics,” Dumford said. Advertisement If you notice that you’re lightheaded because of dehydration from diarrhea or vomiting, you should reach out to a doctor or go to an emergency room ― “you may need IV fluids,” Dumford explained. RUSLANAS BARANAUSKAS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY via Getty Images Norovirus cases are on the rise throughout the country. The virus is extremely contagious, but there are steps you can take to stay well. “It is a very infectious virus,” Troisi said. “It can last on surfaces for up to two weeks, and so it spreads very easily.” Advertisement The best way to lower your chance of getting sick is by simply washing your hands ― and washing them well. “There have been studies about proper hand washing ... a majority of people, including food handlers, do not wash their hands properly,” Troisi said. This doesn’t mean they aren’t washing their hands at all, but are likely not taking off their rings and washing their hands for a full 20 seconds, she said. You should wash your hands for the length of “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” It’s also not good enough to squirt some sanitizer on your hands before sitting down for a meal. “Alcohol hand sanitizers are not effective in killing norovirus,” Dumford said. Advertisement “Hand sanitizer is great for other pathogens like the flu and COVID and other respiratory viruses, but when trying to prevent the acquisition of some gastrointestinal viruses, including norovirus, soap and water is the standard,” Dumford said. You should wash your hands before eating, after using the restroom, after changing diapers and when caring for sick people, according to Troisi. “If you know that there are norovirus outbreaks happening in your community, then even [after] shaking hands you’d want to wash your hands,” she noted. If you do get sick, stay away from other people and monitor for severe symptoms. Washing your hands and other good hygiene habits will lower your chances of getting this vomiting illness but won’t eliminate your chance of getting sick. Advertisement If you do get ill, stay away from other people. “If you have vomiting [or] diarrhea, stay home while still sick,” Dumford said. “Also make sure to wash your hands frequently with soap and water to avoid having norovirus on your hands and then contaminating any shared surfaces.” It’s also a good idea to refrain from cooking for other people for a full two to three days after your symptoms go away, Dumford added. This will help keep those around you healthy. Again, monitor for any red-flag symptoms such as dehydration, fevers and blood in your stool. If you notice any concerning symptoms, seek medical attention. Advertisement According to Troisi, there is a fairly new norovirus strain that’s infecting people and has been since earlier this year. It’s impossible to know what this means for norovirus rates this winter, but “it may be that this year will be a little worse than other years with this new strain,” she said. Outside of those common source outbreaks, such as cruise ships, norovirus is also known as winter vomiting disease,” added Dumford. “We see a usual rise in cases throughout the winter months.” Advertisement The illness seems to spread more easily in cooler temperatures, he added, “and is able to survive longer on surfaces during that period of time.” Norovirus can cause very unpleasant symptoms. Norovirus tends to cause nausea and vomiting, and can also cause fever and diarrhea, Dumford said. Most people are sick for one to three days and recover fine at home, according to Troisi. (Be sure to stay hydrated if you do get sick.) It can last longer, though, and can lead to complications that require medical attention. “If you start to get fevers, blood in your stool, then call your healthcare provider as those can be signs of a more invasive type of gastrointestinal infection that may need antibiotics,” Dumford said. Advertisement If you notice that you’re lightheaded because of dehydration from diarrhea or vomiting, you should reach out to a doctor or go to an emergency room ― “you may need IV fluids,” Dumford explained. RUSLANAS BARANAUSKAS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY via Getty Images Norovirus cases are on the rise throughout the country. The virus is extremely contagious, but there are steps you can take to stay well. “It is a very infectious virus,” Troisi said. “It can last on surfaces for up to two weeks, and so it spreads very easily.” Advertisement The best way to lower your chance of getting sick is by simply washing your hands ― and washing them well. “There have been studies about proper hand washing ... a majority of people, including food handlers, do not wash their hands properly,” Troisi said. This doesn’t mean they aren’t washing their hands at all, but are likely not taking off their rings and washing their hands for a full 20 seconds, she said. You should wash your hands for the length of “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” It’s also not good enough to squirt some sanitizer on your hands before sitting down for a meal. “Alcohol hand sanitizers are not effective in killing norovirus,” Dumford said. Advertisement “Hand sanitizer is great for other pathogens like the flu and COVID and other respiratory viruses, but when trying to prevent the acquisition of some gastrointestinal viruses, including norovirus, soap and water is the standard,” Dumford said. You should wash your hands before eating, after using the restroom, after changing diapers and when caring for sick people, according to Troisi. “If you know that there are norovirus outbreaks happening in your community, then even [after] shaking hands you’d want to wash your hands,” she noted. If you do get sick, stay away from other people and monitor for severe symptoms. Washing your hands and other good hygiene habits will lower your chances of getting this vomiting illness but won’t eliminate your chance of getting sick. Advertisement If you do get ill, stay away from other people. “If you have vomiting [or] diarrhea, stay home while still sick,” Dumford said. “Also make sure to wash your hands frequently with soap and water to avoid having norovirus on your hands and then contaminating any shared surfaces.” It’s also a good idea to refrain from cooking for other people for a full two to three days after your symptoms go away, Dumford added. This will help keep those around you healthy. Again, monitor for any red-flag symptoms such as dehydration, fevers and blood in your stool. If you notice any concerning symptoms, seek medical attention. Advertisement According to Troisi, there is a fairly new norovirus strain that’s infecting people and has been since earlier this year. It’s impossible to know what this means for norovirus rates this winter, but “it may be that this year will be a little worse than other years with this new strain,” she said. analysis.brief_en: On October 1, 2026, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency initiated a recall of Summerhill Market raspberries and products made with raspberries due to possible norovirus contamination. This recall is linked to an outbreak that has sickened at least 76 people across 16 states, according to the CDC. The event is reported as a potential norovirus issue, with no explicit risk level provided. The investigation is ongoing, and the agency is working to determine the extent of contamination and its impact on public health. The recall highlights the importance of food safety measures and the need for further analysis to confirm the presence of norovirus in the affected products.

news.content: News Issues Wellness Beauty Pharma KOREAN SEARCH Search Health Chosun K-Wellness Oyster Season Begins in October: Calcium, Zinc and Food Safety Tips for Norovirus Risk By Choi So Ra Updated 2026/10/01 15:00 October marks the time when oysters begin to fill out, making oyster soup with rice and oyster pancakes popular seasonal delicacies. /Photo=Clipart Korea As cold winds begin to blow, oyster season also gets underway. October marks the time when oysters begin to fill out, making oyster soup with rice and oyster pancakes popular seasonal delicacies. Rich in various nutrients, including protein, zinc, iron and vitamin B12, oysters can also help support immune health. However, eating them raw carries a risk of food poisoning, including norovirus, so caution is needed when consuming them. Here is a look at the health benefits of oysters and precautions to take when eating them. ◇Oysters are nutrient-rich and low in calories Oysters are a food that provides various nutrients even in small amounts. In particular, they are high in calcium and are therefore called the “milk of the sea.” Calcium is a component of bones and teeth, making oysters beneficial for growing children and middle-aged and older adults at high risk of developing osteoporosis. They are also rich in zinc. About 78mg of zinc is contained in 100g of oysters, which exceeds the recommended daily intake for adults. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Home Health Summerhill Market Recalls Frozen Raspberries Over Norovirus Concerns Summerhill Market Recalls Frozen Raspberries Over Norovirus Concerns James Anderson Published Oct 1, 2026 - 11:18 10 Reads Last Update Oct 1, 2026 - 11:18 Share WhatsApp The products (pictured), sold at Summerhill Market are suspected to contain Norovirus. Health Canada Smallest Font Largest Font Canadian food safety authorities issued a province-wide recall on Sept. 29, 2026, for frozen raspberry products sold at Summerhill Market locations across Ontario due to possible norovirus contamination. Explore Food Tech Discover more The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) flagged four specific products under the Summerhill Market brand: frozen raspberries, frozen berry mix, frozen smoothie mix, and Protein Power Pod Raspberries. The affected items were sold between July 29 and Sept. 15, 2026. Retail locations involved in the distribution include five Toronto stores—on Summerhill Avenue, Dundas Street West, Eglinton Avenue West, Mount Pleasant Road, and Bathurst Street—along with a location on Wellington Street West in Aurora. According to federal regulators, the recall resulted from an ongoing investigation into a foodborne illness outbreak, though no confirmed illnesses tied directly to the recalled items have been reported to date. Check Recalls Discover more "Do not consume, use, sell, serve, or distribute recalled products," the Canadian Food Inspection Agency said. Health authorities noted that individuals infected with norovirus typically show symptoms of gastroenteritis within 24 to 48 hours of exposure, though onset can occur as early as 12 hours. "People with norovirus illness usually develop symptoms of gastroenteritis within 24 to 48 hours, but symptoms can start as early as 12 hours after exposure," the Canadian Food Inspection Agency said. The agency highlighted that the illness often begins abruptly and warned that individuals can face re-infection even after recovering. "The illness often begins suddenly. Even after having the illness, you can still become re-infected by norovirus," the Canadian Food Inspection Agency said. Common symptoms include diarrhea, sudden vomiting, nausea, and stomach cramps, alongside low-grade fever, headache, muscle aches, and fatigue. Most individuals recover within one to two days without medical intervention. "Most people feel better within one or two days, with symptoms usually resolving on their own," the Canadian Food Inspection Agency said. Try New Foods Consumers holding the recalled products are advised to dispose of them immediately or return them to the store. news.title_zh: Summerhill Market 因 诺如病毒 问题召回冷冻覆盆子 - SuaraGarut.ID
news.source_body_en: Summerhill Market has issued a recall of frozen raspberry products due to possible norovirus contamination, as confirmed by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA). The affected items include frozen raspberries, frozen berry mix, frozen smoothie mix, and Protein Power Pod Raspberries, which were sold between July 29 and September 29, 2026, at locations across Ontario, including five Toronto stores and one in Aurora. The recall was announced on October 1, 2026, following an ongoing investigation into a foodborne illness outbreak. However, no confirmed illnesses have been directly linked to the recalled products. Health authorities note that norovirus typically causes gastroenteritis with symptoms like diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach cramps, which usually resolve within one to two days without medical intervention. Consumers are advised to dispose of or return the recalled products immediately.
news.content_zh: 经加拿大食品检验局 (CFIA) 证实,Summerhill Market 已召回冷冻覆盆子产品,原因是可能存在 诺如病毒 污染。受影响的商品包括冷冻覆盆子、冷冻浆果混合物、冷冻混合冰沙和 Protein Power Pod Raspberry,这些产品于 2026 年 7 月 29 日至 9 月 29 日期间在安大略省各地销售,其中包括多伦多的 5 家商店和奥罗拉的 1 家商店。此次召回是在对 食源性 疾病 暴发 进行持续调查后于 2026 年 10 月 1 日宣布的。然而,目前还没有确诊的疾病与召回产品直接相关。卫生当局指出,诺如病毒 通常会引起胃肠炎,伴有腹泻、呕吐和胃痉挛等症状,这些症状通常在一到两天内消失,无需医疗干预。建议消费者立即处置或退回召回的产品。
news.summary_zh: 经加拿大食品检验局 (CFIA) 证实,Summerhill Market 已召回冷冻覆盆子产品,原因是可能存在 诺如病毒 污染。受影响的商品包括冷冻覆盆子、冷冻浆果混合物、冷冻混合冰沙和 Protein Power Pod Raspberry,这些产品于 2026 年 7 月 29 日至 9 月 29 日期间在安大略省各地销售,其中包括多伦多的 5 家商店和奥罗拉的 1 家商店。此次召回是在对 食源性 疾病 暴发 进行持续调查后于 2026 年 10 月 1 日宣布的。然而,目前还没有确诊的疾病与召回产品直接相关。卫生当局指出,诺如病毒 通常会引起胃肠炎,伴有腹泻、呕吐和胃痉挛等症状,这些症状通常在一到两天内消失,无需医疗干预。建议消费者立即处置或退回召回的产品。
